interactions: Levetiracetam + sertraline: no pharmacokinetic interaction. Additive sedation is possible; levetiracetam can cause irritability or low mood, relevant with a history of depression.
Lamotrigine + sertraline: no consistent pharmacokinetic interaction; isolated reports describe raised lamotrigine concentrations with sertraline, so watch for dizziness or ataxia during titration.
Carbamazepine + sertraline: carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and markedly lowers sertraline concentrations, with loss of antidepressant effect; phenytoin and phenobarbital act likewise.
Oxcarbazepine + sertraline: weaker CYP3A4 induction may lower sertraline modestly.
Ferrous sulfate: no interaction with levetiracetam, lamotrigine or lacosamide.

output.summary: Levetiracetam, lamotrigine and lacosamide have no relevant pharmacokinetic interaction with sertraline; carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital lower sertraline concentrations.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start carbamazepine or phenytoin as the initial ASM: enzyme induction lowers sertraline and would compromise oncologic drugs if tissue diagnosis requires them.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not attribute the auditory episodes to depression or migraine: they are stereotyped focal seizures.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for no enzyme induction and no interaction with sertraline; with his depression history prefer lamotrigine, or monitor mood closely on levetiracetam.

Refer for epilepsy surgery evaluation of the left posterior superior temporal gyrus lesion: resection gives the tissue diagnosis and the best chance of seizure freedom, and language lateralization and mapping precede it because the lesion lies near posterior temporal language cortex in a left-handed man.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Arrange gastrointestinal evaluation of the iron-deficiency anemia, which persists in an adult man after eight months of oral iron.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (lateral neocortical TLE with auditory aura) due to a left superior temporal gyrus low-grade epilepsy-associated tumor (presumed ganglioglioma, CNS WHO grade 1)

differential.diagnosis: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) with focal temporal epilepsy
differential.key_features: A cortical cystic non-enhancing temporal lesion in a young adult overlaps with ganglioglioma on MRI; only histology separates them.

No enhancement, no restricted diffusion and minimal perilesional edema in a well-circumscribed cystic lesion; the grandfather's tumor of unknown type is not a hereditary risk. Histology closes the question.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD type II) of left temporal neocortex
differential.key_features: The lesion is cystic with a mural nodule, without a transmantle sign or gray-white blurring.
No faciobrachial dystonic seizures, no cognitive decline (recall 3/3), sodium 138 mEq/L; a structural lesion concordant with the EEG explains the seizures.
His depression is in remission; the sounds are brief, stereotyped, lateralized to the right and evolve to impaired awareness, automatisms and a convulsion, with a concordant EEG focus and lesion.
No headache; stereotyped progression to impaired awareness, post-ictal confusion and a structural lesion with a concordant EEG focus.

key_clinical_evidence: A stereotyped auditory aura (music or voices heard from the right) localizes to the left lateral temporal neocortex (superior temporal gyrus), unlike the epigastric, olfactory or deja vu auras of mesial temporal epilepsy.
Right head version, right arm clonic jerking and a transient post-ictal right pronator drift point to the left hemisphere.
The routine EEG shows left mid-to-posterior temporal sharp waves maximal at T5, concordant with the posterior superior temporal gyrus lesion.

The epilepsy-protocol MRI shows a cystic left superior temporal gyrus lesion with a non-enhancing mural nodule and normal hippocampi: a low-grade epilepsy-associated tumor (ganglioglioma or DNET) whose type needs tissue.
Sertraline and possible future oncologic therapy make a non-inducing ASM the right choice.
Iron-deficiency anemia persisting after eight months of oral iron in a man does not explain the seizures but needs its own gastrointestinal evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Iron-deficiency anemia does not cause focal seizures with an auditory aura and a structural temporal lesion. It persists in an adult man despite eight months of oral iron, so it needs gastrointestinal evaluation in its own right, outside the seizure work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of a single, unknown brain tumor in an elderly grandfather is not an established hereditary risk factor for ganglioglioma (CNS WHO grade 1 developmental tumors, not familial); the MRI absence of enhancement and restricted diffusion is more diagnostically informative than this family history.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

additional_observations: Technique: 3T MRI, dedicated epilepsy protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at 1 mm, high-resolution coronal T2 perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, DWI, SWI). Post-contrast T1 sequences were added by the reviewing radiologist because a lesion was seen.

mri.impression: Well-circumscribed cystic left superior temporal gyrus lesion (2.1 x 1.7 x 1.9 cm) with an eccentric non-enhancing mural nodule. Imaging features are most consistent with a low-grade cystic neoplasm; ganglioglioma and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) are the leading considerations. A higher-grade primary glial tumor cannot be fully excluded without tissue sampling, though the absence of enhancement, restricted diffusion, and perilesional edema favors a low-grade neoplastic or cortical dysplasia-spectrum entity. No hippocampal signal abnormality or sclerosis. Tissue diagnosis recommended.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: lateral neocortical TLE with auditory aura is a less common subtype requiring recognition that T5 EEG focus (posterior temporal) indicates neocortical rather than mesial onset; structural MRI lesion requires characterization with contrast to exclude high-grade glioma; three grounded red herrings (iron deficiency anemia, family history of brain tumor, sertraline taper) may misdirect workup; drug interaction complexity with sertraline and non-enzyme-inducing AED selection.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Two required steps (epilepsy-protocol MRI and routine EEG); recognizing the lateral neocortical auditory aura and the posterior temporal EEG focus, characterizing the lesion, choosing a non-inducing ASM with sertraline, and three grounded distractors (iron deficiency, family history of a brain tumor, sertraline taper) add decision complexity.
metadata.real_seed_note: Case is authored as a clinically authentic representation of lateral neocortical temporal lobe epilepsy due to ganglioglioma, based on established clinical literature (gangliogliomas are the most common tumor-associated epilepsy in young adults, frequently presenting with auditory aura from superior temporal gyrus lesions). PMID search for a directly matching open-access PMC case was conducted; no single PMC CC-BY case was retrieved and verified at authoring time. patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Ramirez is a 34-year-old left-handed man with a history of prior depression and iron-deficiency anemia who presents to the neurology inpatient service following a witnessed focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure at his apartment yesterday evening. His partner reports that over the past five months, Mr. Ramirez has been experiencing stereotyped episodes beginning with him suddenly pausing, appearing startled, and then saying he hears fragments of music or unintelligible voices 'coming from the right side.' These auditory phenomena typically last 10–20 seconds, sometimes followed by a rising sense of apprehension. On approximately half of these occasions, the auditory aura progresses: he loses awareness, turns his head to the right, and performs repetitive fumbling movements with his right hand lasting 30–60 seconds, after which he is briefly confused. He has been having these episodes 2–3 times per week for the past 5 months. He initially attributed the auditory experiences to his depression and did not seek medical attention. Yesterday's episode followed the same auditory aura but evolved into sustained right-arm clonic jerking and then generalized tonic-clonic convulsions lasting approximately 90 seconds, after which he was confused and sleepy for 20 minutes. His partner called emergency services. He was found post-ictally with a right palmar abrasion from a fall.

On further questioning, Mr. Ramirez confirms that all episodes begin identically — a clear, stereotyped auditory sensation he now recognizes as an aura. He denies olfactory aura, epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu, or ictal fear. He denies any recent illness, fever, rash, or systemic symptoms. He is not on any antiepileptic medications. He was previously on sertraline 100 mg daily for depression, which was tapered to 50 mg six weeks ago as he is in remission, and his psychiatrist is planning further tapering. He mentions that his grandfather died of a brain tumor of unknown type, which has been a source of anxiety since the seizures began. He has not had any brain imaging in the past. On review of systems, he denies headaches, visual disturbances, focal weakness (aside from the post-ictal right pronator drift noted on arrival), or any constitutional symptoms. Formal audiological history is unremarkable; he has no tinnitus or hearing loss.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration. Small abrasion on the right palm consistent with a fall during the seizure. No papilledema on fundoscopy. No lymphadenopathy.

Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with volitional activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally on finger-rub testing. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal heel-to-toe gait. Tandem walk intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal prosody. No paraphasic errors. Naming and repetition intact. Recalls 3/3 words at five minutes. Serial sevens performed correctly. Informal bedside phonemic processing appears intact. Mild anxiety noted during history-taking but appropriate to clinical context.

neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
